history.heading: Bronze Age civilisations
paragraphs: Greece is home to the earliest advanced civilisations in Europe. The Minoans on Crete built the palace of Knossos and flourished in the 2nd millennium BCE, followed by the Mycenaeans on the mainland, whose world is reflected in Homer's Iliad and Odyssey.

history.heading: Classical Greece
paragraphs: From the 8th century BCE, independent city-states such as Athens, Sparta, Corinth and Thebes developed, and Greek colonies spread across the Mediterranean. The first Olympic Games are traditionally dated to 776 BCE. The Greeks defeated Persian invasions at Marathon (490 BCE) and Salamis (480 BCE).

In the 5th century BCE, Athens developed democracy and became a centre of culture under Pericles, building the Parthenon. Philosophers such as Socrates, Plato and Aristotle, historians Herodotus and Thucydides, and dramatists such as Sophocles laid foundations of Western thought. Alexander the Great of Macedon conquered an empire stretching to India, spreading Greek culture across the Hellenistic world.

history.heading: Roman, Byzantine and Ottoman rule
paragraphs: Rome conquered Greece in the 2nd century BCE but adopted much of its culture. The eastern Roman Empire, known as the Byzantine Empire, was Greek-speaking and Orthodox Christian, with its capital at Constantinople, for over a thousand years.
After Constantinople fell to the Ottomans in 1453, most of Greece remained under Ottoman rule for nearly four centuries, while the Orthodox Church preserved Greek identity.

history.heading: Modern Greece
paragraphs: The Greek War of Independence began in 1821, supported by European powers and romantic philhellenes such as Lord Byron, and Greece became independent in 1830. It expanded its territory over the following century. A 1923 population exchange with Turkey followed a disastrous war in Asia Minor.

Greece suffered a brutal Nazi occupation in the Second World War, then a civil war from 1946 to 1949. A military junta ruled from 1967 to 1974. After democracy was restored and the monarchy abolished, Greece joined the European Community in 1981 and adopted the euro in 2001. A severe debt crisis from 2009 led to international bailouts and years of austerity.

culture.heading: Language and faith
paragraphs: Greek is one of the oldest recorded living languages, written in the Greek alphabet, which inspired the Latin and Cyrillic alphabets. The Greek Orthodox Church is central to national identity, and Easter is the most important holiday.
Greece has many UNESCO World Heritage Sites, including the Acropolis of Athens, Delphi, Olympia, Mount Athos and the monasteries of Meteora.

culture.heading: Food and daily life
paragraphs: The Mediterranean diet is recognised by UNESCO. Greek cuisine includes olive oil, feta cheese, moussaka, souvlaki, gyros, Greek salad and baklava, with ouzo as a traditional drink.

Music includes rebetiko, a blues-like urban genre, and traditional dances such as the sirtaki. Social life revolves around the kafeneio (coffee house) and the taverna. Football and basketball are popular, and Greece won the European football championship in 2004.

politics.heading: Parliamentary republic
paragraphs: Greece is a parliamentary republic. The prime minister leads the government, responsible to the single-chamber Hellenic Parliament, while the president, elected by parliament, has a largely ceremonial role.

The centre-right New Democracy party has governed since 2019. Greece is a member of the EU, the eurozone and NATO. Relations with Türkiye over maritime borders in the Aegean and Cyprus are a long-standing source of tension. A 2018 agreement resolved a name dispute with North Macedonia.

economy.heading: Tourism and shipping
paragraphs: Tourism is a major pillar of the economy, with tens of millions of visitors to islands such as Santorini, Mykonos and Crete and to ancient sites. Greek shipowners control one of the largest merchant fleets in the world. Agriculture produces olive oil, fruits and vegetables, and Greece is a major exporter of refined petroleum products.

economy.heading: Recovery from crisis
paragraphs: The debt crisis of 2009–2018 caused the economy to shrink by about a quarter and unemployment to soar, and many young Greeks emigrated. Since then, the economy has recovered, unemployment has fallen and Greece regained investment-grade credit ratings in 2023, though public debt remains among the highest in the EU.
